speaker: Doctor
text: I am Dr. Agent. Please describe your symptoms in detail; specifically, when did your dizziness, nausea, and imbalance begin, and do you feel like the room is spinning or are you just off-balance?

speaker: Patient
text: 27-year-old male. The patient reports a sustained sensation of the room spinning since this morning, which is low grade and constant. He occasionally feels nauseous and has taken diphenhydramine to help him sleep, which also alleviates his symptoms slightly. He mentions recent increased intake of garlic due to trying to recover from a cold a few days ago. Past medical history is unremarkable.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Vestibular Neuritis. The sustained spinning sensation (vertigo) lasting since this morning, accompanied by nausea and partial relief from diphenhydramine, strongly suggests an inner ear inflammation affecting the vestibular nerve, rather than a transient episode like benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) or a central cause like a stroke. The recent garlic intake and cold history are likely coincidental or a minor trigger for an underlying viral etiology, but the clinical picture is classic for vestibular neuritis. I will confirm this with a Dix-Hallpike maneuver and an HINTS exam to rule out central causes.
